## How the New Zealand Health System Works

New Zealand's health system is a mix of publicly funded and privately funded services, designed to ensure all New Zealanders have access to care — though access and affordability remain ongoing challenges.

### The National Organisation: Health New Zealand

In 2022, the former Labour-led government undertook what was described as the biggest shake-up of New Zealand's health system in a generation, replacing 20 district health boards with a single national body, Health New Zealand (also known as Te Whatu Ora). [[1]](cite://1/1) The aim was to reduce fragmentation, improve consistency of care across the country, and eliminate the so-called "postcode lottery" where the quality of care depended on where you lived. [[2]](cite://2/1)[[1]](cite://1/2)

Since then, the organisation has faced significant financial and governance challenges, including a $1.3 billion projected deficit and debates over staffing, wait times, and access to primary care. [[2]](cite://2/2) A commissioner was appointed in 2024 to address these issues, with reducing wait times named as the most urgent priority. [[2]](cite://2/3)

The Ministry of Health retains oversight of Health New Zealand and is responsible for setting policy and funding levels. [[3]](cite://3/1)

### Primary Care: Your GP

The front door to the health system for most New Zealanders is their general practitioner (GP), accessed through local medical centres. [[4]](cite://4/1) Doctors in New Zealand are private practitioners, meaning they charge fees for consultations, though government subsidies help reduce the cost. [[4]](cite://4/2)[[5]](cite://5/1)

Some key points about accessing a GP:

- Around 96% of New Zealanders are enrolled with a GP clinic. [[6]](cite://6/1)
- Despite this, about one in five adults reported being unable to get care from their regular GP or nurse when needed, mainly due to long waits, staff shortages, or clinic closures, according to a 2025 Health Quality & Safety Commission survey. [[1]](cite://1/3)
- Between one-quarter and one-third of people have put off visiting a doctor or collecting a prescription because of cost. [[7]](cite://7/1)
- The GP workforce is under pressure, with a shortage predicted to grow to 1,000 GPs by 2033. [[6]](cite://6/2)

### Subsidies and Free Care

Not everyone pays the same amount to see a doctor. Subsidies apply to lower-income New Zealanders, and from July 2015, over 90% of general practices offered zero-fee visits to children aged 13 and under. [[8]](cite://8/1) The $5 per item prescription charge was also removed for that age group. [[8]](cite://8/2)

Prescription medicines for adults come with part-charges, but many drugs are purchased in bulk by the government's medicines-buying agency, Pharmac (Pharmaceutical Management Agency), helping to keep costs relatively low. [[4]](cite://4/3)[[9]](cite://9/1)

### Hospitals

Public hospitals are funded by central government and provide emergency and advanced medical care free of charge. [[9]](cite://9/2) There are also private, fee-charging hospitals, used mostly for non-urgent surgery. [[9]](cite://9/3) As of the late 1990s, around 38% of New Zealanders held private health insurance, primarily to cover non-urgent surgical procedures. [[9]](cite://9/4)

Private health insurance has been available since 1962, when the Southern Cross Medical Care Society was established, and a number of other insurers have since entered the market. [[10]](cite://10/1)

### Telehealth: A New Way to Access Care

As GP shortages have grown, the government launched a new 24/7 telehealth service in July 2025, allowing New Zealanders to book online appointments with doctors and nurse practitioners from anywhere in the country. [[11]](cite://11/1) The service is intended to bridge the gap when a timely in-person GP appointment isn't available. [[12]](cite://12/1)

In its first few months, the service recorded over 21,000 consultations for more than 19,000 people. [[12]](cite://12/2) Doctors and nurse practitioners using the service can assess symptoms, diagnose conditions, prescribe medications, and provide referrals. [[11]](cite://11/2)

However, some health professionals have raised concerns about telehealth replacing in-person care for complex or chronic conditions, noting that face-to-face consultations remain the "gold standard" for ongoing health needs. [[12]](cite://12/3)

### Dental Care

Dental care operates on a mixed public-private model. Children and adolescents up to 18 years of age receive free dental care, but adults must pay for their own treatment, though some funding exists for emergency dental care. [[13]](cite://13/1)

### Māori Health

Māori and Pacific communities continue to face greater barriers to accessing healthcare, including affordability and availability. [[1]](cite://1/4) The 2022 reforms created a Māori Health Authority to embed Treaty-based governance, but it was disestablished by the incoming government in 2024 — a decision that remains contested. [[1]](cite://1/5)

Free kaupapa Māori (Māori-centred) hauora (health and wellbeing) clinics exist in some communities, providing nurse-led care to those who cannot access or afford mainstream GP services. [[14]](cite://14/1)

Would you like to know more about how to find and enrol with a GP clinic near you, or about the telehealth services now available?

It covers the nation's diverse population of over 5 million people, including 67% of European descent, significant Māori (565,329), Pacific Islander, and Asian communities. Demographic trends reveal an aging population, declining birth rates, and increasing ethnic diversity concentrated primarily in the North Island, particularly Auckland. The document details family structures, housing trends showing declining home ownership (from 73.8% in 1991 to 67.8% in 2001), and rising single-parent families (31% in 2001). Gender dynamics highlight women's improved economic and social status since the 1980s, alongside New Zealand's progressive LGBTQ+ rights stance, including decriminalization of homosexuality (1986), civil unions (2005), and same-sex marriage (2013). [Page 18] Rural hospitals The first New Zealand hospitals were in the main towns, so country people needing urgent surgery could face a long, painful journey. Gradually more hospitals and maternity homes were set up in the regions, often part funded by local contributions or rates. In 1885 the country was divided into hospital districts, each controlled by a board. These districts multiplied, and at one stage there were 47. In the 1960s the number was reduced, and some smaller general and maternity hospitals closed. Health reforms in the 1980s and 1990s also led to the demise of some small rural hospitals, and surgical services were cut at others. In 2001, 21 district health boards were set up, and the smallest rural hospital board districts disappeared. In 2008 there were 36 rural hospitals in New Zealand.

3.document_title: Rural Services in New Zealand: Infrastructure, Communications, Health, and Emergency Services Development
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines rural services development in New Zealand from the 1840s through the early 2000s. It covers transportation networks including roads, railways, and motor vehicles that connected farming regions to markets. Electricity expansion from urban lighting in the 1920s to 80% farm access by 1936, with further rural electrification between 1948-1965, fundamentally transformed agricultural practices. Communications infrastructure evolved through postal services, telegraph, telephone, radio, television, and internet systems serving remote communities. Health services development included country GPs, rural hospitals, Plunket services, dental care, and air ambulance services. Emergency and welfare services evolved from local bucket brigades to organized fire services, police services adapted for isolated areas, and welfare initiatives like the Bush Nurse and Emergency Housekeeper Scheme established in 1927. Government prioritization, private enterprise, and technological advancement collectively modernized agricultural practices, improved rural living standards, and reshaped New Zealand's economic landscape.

4.document_title: Te Hauora Māori: A Comprehensive History of Māori Health in New Zealand from Pre-European Times to the 20th Century
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori health across multiple centuries, from pre-European times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Before European contact, Māori were generally fit and healthy with life expectancy around 28-30 years, relying on traditional healing practices involving tohunga (healers), rongoā rākau (plant medicines), and karakia (rituals). European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Despite vaccination campaigns and health education, tuberculosis, typhoid, and the 1918 influenza pandemic devastated Māori communities. The 1938 Social Security Act introduced free hospital admission and universal medical benefits. Post-WWII improvements included successful tuberculosis campaigns and declining infant mortality rates. However, significant health disparities persisted throughout the 20th century, with Māori mortality rates approximately twice that of non-Māori in 1960. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

5.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines care provision in New Zealand across multiple populations and service areas. It traces the historical evolution from 19th-century benevolent institutions through contemporary practices, covering aged care, disability support, hospice and palliative care, and family caregiving. The document details the shift from institutional models to community-based "ageing in place" policies, documenting residential facilities, support services like Meals on Wheels, home care, and retirement villages. It examines the hospice movement from early institutions like St Joseph's Home (1899) and Mary Potter Hospice (1979) to modern comprehensive services. The document addresses care for people with disabilities, tracing the transition from family responsibility through institutionalization to modern community-based support following key legislation like the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act 1975 and Funded Family Care (2013). It highlights the critical role of unpaid carers—predominantly women—and discusses challenges including stress, financial impact, and social isolation. Contemporary policy issues examined include funding equity for family carers, staffing shortages, low wages for care workers, inequitable rural-urban service distribution, and residential care standards. The document emphasizes integrated care approaches and notes the landmark equal pay case of Kristine Bartlett.

6.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of health practitioners in New Zealand, covering their historical development, regulation, workforce composition, and cultural considerations. It traces the evolution from 19th-century doctors, nurses, and pharmacists to the diverse range of regulated health professions in the 21st century. Key topics include: medical training and specialization (first medical school in Dunedin 1875, second in Auckland 1968); professionalization of nursing and midwifery; regulation through the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003; and consumer rights frameworks. Significant workforce trends include feminization of medicine (7% female doctors in 1930s to 42% in 2015), reliance on overseas-trained doctors (40% of workforce), and underrepresentation of Māori and Pacific practitioners. The document details GP distribution across regions (105 per 100,000 in Auckland to 61 on West Coast), nursing evolution from untrained workers to regulated professionals through the 1901 Nurses Registration Act, and transition from hospital-based to institutional nursing education completed in 1989. Midwifery evolved from unregulated practice to autonomous professional status following the 1990 Nurses Amendment Act, with 75% of women choosing midwives as lead maternity carers. Allied health practitioners including pharmacists (4,279 registered in 2025), physiotherapists, acupuncturists, and chiropractors are covered. The nursing workforce comprises over half the total health workforce with 52,729 nurses holding practising certificates in 2015, while 3,068 midwives were registered that year. The document examines alternative and complementary medicine, and representation of Māori and Pacific health practitioners. Cultural safety is explained as a framework developed in nursing and midwifery to ensure culturally appropriate healthcare, first formalized in 1989.

[Page 1] Health practitioners ByAllison Kirkman In the 19th century doctors, nurses and pharmacists were the main health practitioners in New Zealand, but since then many new types of health care have developed. New Zealand has laws requiring health practitioners to follow professional guidelines. Doctors At first most doctors were general practitioners (GPs). They had to train overseas until the University of Otago's Medical School opened in Dunedin in 1875. In 1968 a second medical school opened in Auckland. Doctors have specialised in different types of medicine, such as paediatrics (the treatment of children) and psychiatry. Until the 1970s most doctors were men, but by the 2000s more women than men studied medicine. Doctors often have heavy workloads. Some areas find it difficult to hire doctors. In the early 21st century around 40% of the doctors in New Zealand were from overseas. Nurses and midwives At first nurses did housework and looked after children as well as nursing. They trained on the job and did not need qualifications. But after 1901 nurses had to pass an examination and be registered to practise. In the 1970s and 1980s nurse training shifted from hospitals to polytechnics and universities. After 1904 midwives trained in hospitals. From the 1920s to 1990 midwives were trained nurses, and from 1971 to 1990 they could not deliver a baby without a doctor present. In the 21st century people can train as midwives without being a nurse, and midwives can deliver babies on their own. Other health practitioners In other areas chiropractic, dentistry, dietetics, medical laboratory science, medical radiation technology, occupational therapy, optometry and optical dispensing, osteopathy, pharmacy, physiotherapy, podiatry, psychology and psychotherapy practitioners also have to follow practising guidelines. Māori and Pacific health practitioners Although Māori were 14.9% of the population in 2013, and Pacific people were 7.4%, only 2.7% of doctors and 6.5% of nurses were Māori in 2015, and only 1.8% of doctors and 2.6% of nurses were Pacific people.

This comprehensive document provides an overview of public health in New Zealand, covering disease prevention, health promotion, and population-level health inequalities from the 19th century to present. It traces the evolution of public health infrastructure, including the Department of Public Health (established 1900) and its transformation into the Ministry of Health, with major reforms in 1993 and the 2000s emphasizing district health boards.

9.document_title: New Zealand's Threatened Species: Conservation Status, Strategies, and Recovery Efforts
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

[Page 7] Health insurance Insuring against injury or illness was one of the most important functions of the early New Zealand based friendly societies, based on 19th century English models. In 1938 the Social Security Act provided for means tested old age pensions and reduced the need for individuals to insure against illness or depend entirely on savings or charity. Although state funded health care was available to everyone in New Zealand, private medical insurance became available when the Southern Cross Medical Care Society was incorporated in 1962. A number of other life and general companies later entered the health insurance field.

10.document_title: Insurance in New Zealand: Comprehensive History, Development, and Transformation from Colonial Times to the 21st Century
10.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of insurance in New Zealand from early colonial times through the early 21st century, covering life insurance, general insurance, accident insurance, and disaster coverage. Early colonial New Zealand faced significant risks including shipwrecks, fires, and workplace accidents, driving rapid insurance industry growth. The government established Government Life Insurance in 1869 and State Fire Insurance Office in 1903 to provide affordable coverage. The document details accident insurance development from the early 1900s, motor vehicle insurance following widespread car availability, and the 1972 Accident Compensation Commission that replaced litigation. Disaster insurance evolution is examined through major events including the 1931 Napier earthquake and creation of the Earthquake and War Damage Commission (1944), later becoming the Natural Hazards Commission in 2024. The 20th century witnessed significant structural transformations including the shift from commission agents to insurance brokers, blurring of boundaries between life and general insurance sectors, and major takeovers and privatization following 1980s economic reforms. Government Life became Tower Corporation and was eventually privatized, while State Insurance was sold to Norwich Union Holdings. Modern developments saw branch offices decline as telephone and internet services replaced face-to-face interactions. By 2007-8, the industry earned over $3 billion in gross income, with general insurance premiums exceeding $3 billion and life insurance premiums reaching $1.48 billion.

11.text:
[Page 6] Some parts of New Zealand are better supplied with doctors than others. In 2014 the Auckland District Health Board area had 105 GPs per 100,000 population and the Lakes District had 90, compared to 65 in Counties Manukau and 61 on the West Coast. Rural practices and hospitals often struggle to attract doctors because of high workloads and difficulty accessing ongoing vocational training. Both the Otago and Auckland medical schools allocate places for rural students because they are more likely to practise in rural districts than their urban counterparts.

21.document_title: A Plague on All Our Houses: How Bubonic Plague Shaped New Zealand's Health System
21.document_summary: In 1900, bubonic plague arrived in New Zealand via infected rats discovered in Auckland, coinciding with a pandemic spreading from China through Australia. Health commissioners James Mason and John Gilruth investigated poor sanitary conditions and faced resistance from business owners reluctant to report infected rodents. Despite public skepticism following a false alarm, a confirmed plague death in June 1900 prompted quarantine measures. Over the following years, 21 cases and 9 deaths were recorded, with the last in 1911. The outbreak's silver lining was transformative: it prompted the Public Health Act 1900, replacing ineffective local boards with a forward-looking Department of Public Health, establishing modern disease control infrastructure in New Zealand.

[Page 5] If New Zealand’s experience of the 1918 influenza pandemic can be said to have had an upside, it was this: it triggered the passing, soon after, of a new Health Act claimed by many as the best of its kind in the English speaking world. It was a growing concern at the likelihood of another such pandemic—and a realisation that neither the World Health Organization nor individual governments were taking the prospect seriously—that, in 1996, prompted Jennings to sketch out a contingency plan. “I still have the envelope I drew it up on,” he told me. Jennings then found himself charged with formalising New Zealand’s influenza control and pandemic preparedness strategies, which were among the first in the world. [Page 1] 'Totally bloated': New Health NZ Te Whatu Ora boss Lester Levy lays into bureaucracy 2024 07 23 13:48:38+12:00 Health NZ Te Whatu Ora's new commissioner Lester Levy. The new Commissioner of Health NZ Te Whatu Ora says his top priority is reducing waiting times, and he also wants to boost productivity and compassion. The government on Monday announced Professor Lester Levy, who had been brought in as chair of the organisation at the end of May, would replace the board as a commissioner. Health Minister Shane Reti had said this was a response to serious concerns about oversight, overspend, and a significant deterioration in financial outlook, with Health NZ now spending $130 million a month over its budget heading towards a $1.3b deficit by the end of the financial year. He also brought in changes to add four regional deputy chief executives, to devolve decisions on healthcare to a more local level. Levy said a lot of the government's announcement yesterday which included a lot focused on finances, but he took on the role for three reasons: wait times, productivity and compassion. "Our most urgent and critical priority is to reduce waiting times," he told reporters in Auckland on Tuesday morning. Second, a lot more healthcare could be delivered out of the resources being provided, he said. "Productivity is not an economic or financial construct .... productivity is a clinical construct." Finally, he wanted Health New Zealand to be more compassionate and caring. "We want to be consistent that every person actually gets this." He said the $1.3b deficit was "entirely unacceptable, because never before has there been so much money invested into healthcare, never before have we had so many FTEs". He said Health NZ was a big organisation, but in his view it is "totally bloated" with bureaucracy. It would be a challenge to resolve but it would be resolved, he said, and then the organisation would focus all its attention on patients. Health NZ was formed when the previous Labour government merged 20 District Health Boards, aiming to reduce costs and duplication and eliminating the 'post code lottery' of inconsistent care across different regions. Chief executive Margie Apa said the organisation now had some resources it did not have when it started, and to focus on delivering care in the regions. Margie Apa She says the change will push responsibilities and accountabilities for budgets into the regions, as well as looking at how resources and staffing was managed. Merging 29 entities was never going to be fully achieved in the first two years, Apa said particularly when they were dealing with Covid during the first couple of years but there was now an opportunity to ensure the different regions had a voice in the way care was delivered. Political storm rages The political rhetoric around Levy's appointment has continued to focus on who takes the blame for the budget blow out. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon could not say exactly how much an extra 2500 back office staff had cost, but was confident the extra bureaucracy had contributed to costs. He said the agency had a $30 billion budget to manage and that had not been done well. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon "So there's a financial performance issue, but importantly there's also an organisational performance issue in terms of what has been put together as a restructure, what has created large amounts of bureaucracy and management." Luxon said there was also a third issue a lack of healthcare targets and outcomes. He had on Monday put the blame on the previous Labour government's approach to its health reform programme. However, Labour has continued to hit back against those accusations, saying a financial blow out "in the financial year that they are responsible for is [the coalition's] responsibility". Labour leader Chris Hipkins told reporters at Parliament on Tuesday the government was overstating its intervention at Health New Zealand, saying the suggestion it had sacked the board was "interesting spin" given five of the seven board members had already quit. He told reporters it was a big shift in power to just one person. Labour leader Chris Hipkins "It's a bit ironic that they're saying the system has become too centralised, when they've now gone to the ultimate centralisation model where they've now got one person doing the job that used to be done by many." He said the government was manufacturing problems to justify its own Budget decisions. Health Minister Dr Shane Reti was clear in his view Health NZ was overspending, and had a lack of oversight. He told RNZ the overspending was due to back office staffing, outsourcing of personnel, poor procurement processes for supplies including inventory on expired stock, as well as inflation and population growth. It included things like 2500 administrative backoffice staff being added to the payroll since 2018 with no notable improvements to the health metrics, he said and part of the problem had been that no one was watching. "This is what the Office of the Auditor General said as well .... there was no internal performance monitoring framework, no one was looking, no one was watching until it became so bad that it suddenly raised a flag up the flag pole and Health NZ became aware of this." Health Minister Shane Reti He said some of the recruitment had been into areas where it was needed least, and not into priority areas such as mental health, maternity, and critical care. Health New Zealand also had not been sharing financial information and board papers with the ministry, he said. "Part of the issue was Health NZ wasn't sharing. They refused to share information with the Minister, and with the Ministry of Health, and actually with Treasury. "Minister Willis and I had to be quite firm early in this year: 'you will share information with your legislative steward the ministry of health, oh, and by the way, with Treasury." In a statement issued as National's spokesperson for Health, Dr Reti claimed Labour was "reinventing history". "This is not a matter of there not being enough funding," he said. "When National and Labour released their strategy for health in the 2023 election, both parties had exactly the same figure an additional $12.57 billion for Health NZ over the forecast period. National has gone even further and invested a record $16.7 billion in the [three budgets to 2026] for Health New Zealand, plus an additional $604 million for more medicines." However, Labour's Ayesha Verrall said this was a major misunderstanding of his own Budget. "Following the election, new estimates of cost inflation and of population growth were made and those were not funded by this government that's why there's a deficit." She said the government owed the public an explanation, and perhaps Health NZ should reinstate the DHB approach of publishing monthly accounts and the breakdown of staff and costs. The board meetings should also be public, she said. Labour's health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall "I have said repeatedly that those meetings should be public, they were made public while Labour was in government and then they reverted to being predominantly in private since the government's changed, which is odd because Shane Reti campaigned on them being public as well." Asked about Levy's track record, she said she would judge him on the job he had been appointed to now. "I'm not in the habit of slagging off public servants who decide to do service for our country. I think the exiting board of Te Whatu Ora has been treated shabbily, I am going to judge Lester Levy on the decisions he makes in this role now." Health advocates warn of underfunding Executive director Sarah Dalton, from the Association of Senior Medical Specialists senior doctors union, questioned the government's $130m a month overspend claim, saying her organisation saw an understaffed system. Association of Senior Medical Specialists executive director Sarah Dalton "I'm in the middle of meetings with our members all over the country, and there is not a single service that is well staffed and that is able to provide the kind of care the people of New Zealand want and expect to be able to access in our health system. So taking to our health budgets with an axe does not seem an appropriate response when we do not have enough doctors, nurses, or allied health workers or the people who support them to do their work." She said the health system was not adequately funded, which was a major part of the problem. Her organisation had done a "deep dive" into this year's health budget provisions and found there was very little new money, with lots of smoke and mirrors in the way it had been presented. Former chair of Te Whatu Ora Rob Campbell who was fired from the agency's board last year after making politicised comments about the National Party said he agreed with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon that they could not keep putting money into a system which was not working. He said the issues in Te Whatu Ora were, however, much wider than just financial or governance control. Campbell said he believed there were issues of mis management and underfunding, but the government should be looking at the Ministry of Health to find out why the system was not working. He said the Ministry of Health was the key element in setting targets for Te Whatu Ora, setting its budget and allocating money, and had presided over the running down of the health system over many years. It had now devised and was running the new system, he said. "The Minister of Health remains the steward of the new system and the key element in setting policy and the amount of funding that is available. The Ministry of Health is the place they should be looking to say 'why isn't this working, and why haven't we been told'." Rob Campbell Verrall said the issue came back to the government's choices, and this year's Budget did not fund the health system in line with inflation. "Predictably, in a country with increasing population and inflation in the health sector, they are now behind where they need to be in terms of funding the health system to keep up with demand." She said it was impossible to cut $1.4b without affecting frontline services.

[Page 1] [repub:theconversation] Arshad Ali and Ehtasham Ghauri Did NZ's sweeping health reforms deliver on their promise? [the_conversation_tracker] https://counter.theconversation.com/content/ 272262/count.gif?distributor=republish lightbox advanced The future of NZ's health reforms now depend as much on politics as on policy. File photo. When the former Labour led government unveiled the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) reforms in 2022, it billed them as the biggest shakeup of New Zealand's health system in a generation. The sweeping overhaul promised to end chronic fragmentation and narrow postcode based gaps in care, and to tackle long standing health inequities. Three years on and with a change in government what can we say that it delivered? We explored this question in a soon to be published analysis and found that the picture is mixed. While national co ordination has improved crisis response and planning, everyday access to primary care especially GP appointments has become harder for many people. The shift in political direction has also revealed a deeper lesson: structural reform can build capacity, but without durable political consensus and clear accountability, any gains in equity remain fragile. What did the reforms actually change? The reforms replaced 20 district health boards with a single national organisation, Health New Zealand, and created a Māori Health Authority to embed Treaty based governance and commissioning. It was a major milestone in New Zealand, recognising Māori leadership in the health system and te Tiriti partnership. The aim was straightforward. A more centralised system could plan better, respond faster in crises and deliver more consistent services across the country. In some respects, we found the reforms have worked. Central co ordination has strengthened winter planning, workforce pay equity, procurement, and the ability to move patients and resources across regions during periods of pressure. During major weather events and seasonal surges, such as Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023, the health system has been better able to function as a single, coordinated entity rather than a collection of disconnected local services. Nonetheless, these improvements have not translated into better access to everyday primary care, leaving a gap that is now at the centre of public concern. General practice has become the front line test of whether the reforms are working, and the 2024 decision to disband the Māori Health Authority has added a further stress test of the system's resilience. According to the 2025 Health Quality & Safety Commission survey, about one in five adults could not get care from their regular GP or nurse when they needed. This was mainly due to long waits, staff shortages or clinic closures. Delays at the primary care level push more people into emergency departments, increasing pressure on hospitals. Low income groups, especially Māori and Pacific communities, are particularly affected, reflecting the ongoing inequities the reforms aimed to address. While some health indicators have improved after the reforms, access to primary care remains uneven, with affordability and availability continuing to determine who receives timely treatment. These figures make GP access a key indicator of whether the system is delivering on its promises. More specifically, this pattern exposes a key limitation of the reforms: centralisation can improve coordination, but it does not guarantee accessibility, affordability or a sustainable funding model for general practice. In other words, the levers that shape people's everyday experience of the system were never fully addressed. Why GP access remains the real test Those issues sit largely outside the structural changes of 2022 reforms, yet they shape how people experience the health system day to day. Equity was meant to be a central defining feature of the reforms, particularly through the establishment of the Māori Health Authority. The objective was to provide authority to Māori people in health policy making, commissioning services, and shaping their priorities. However, the decision to disestablish the Māori Health Authority in 2024 highlighted a core challenge in New Zealand's health reforms. Supporters argue that a single system improves efficiency and clarity. Critics argue it shows equity was never securely embedded but remained politically contingent. The Waitangi Tribunal found the Crown failed to meet its Treaty obligations in the way the authority was revoked. Regardless of one's political stance, the removal of this authority exposes a deeper problem: reforms based on contested governance, without broad political backing, are always at risk of being reversed. Consequently, the change of government has exposed how fragile reform can be when it lacks bipartisan backing and durable accountability mechanisms. When governance arrangements shift with each election cycle, continuity suffers, and so does public trust. None of this means the 2022 reforms were misguided. They responded to real and well documented problems. The pre reform system was more fragmented, inconsistent and often confusing for patients and providers alike. Centralisation has reduced duplication and improved national oversight in ways that were difficult under the old model. However, the past three years show that structural reform alone does not guarantee equity or access. Health systems transform slowly, and outcomes are shaped more by funding, workforce capacity, incentives and political stability than by organisational charts. For most New Zealanders, the success of the reforms will not be judged by how well agencies align at the centre, but by whether they can see a GP when they need one, afford that visit, and avoid ending up in hospital as a result. On that measure, the reforms remain unfinished, and their future now depends as much on politics as on policy. * Arshad Ali is a researcher at the University of Otago and Ehtasham Ghauri is a principal lecturer. 46.document_summary: New Zealand's 2022 Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) health reforms promised to end fragmentation and address health inequities through centralisation. Three years later, results are mixed. While national coordination has improved crisis response and planning, primary care access—particularly GP appointments—has worsened for many, especially low-income and Māori/Pacific communities. The reforms replaced 20 district health boards with Health New Zealand and created a Māori Health Authority for Treaty-based governance. Central coordination strengthened winter planning and workforce equity, but failed to address affordability and accessibility issues. The 2024 decision to disband the Māori Health Authority exposed how fragile reforms are without bipartisan political backing. Structural reform alone cannot guarantee equity; success depends on funding, workforce capacity, and political stability. For most New Zealanders, the reforms' success will be judged by GP access and affordability, not organizational alignment.

A Te Whatu Ora/ Health NZ boss says up to half of all GP work could be done by telehealth including by overseas based doctors. Martin Hefford The agency's director of living well Martin Hefford was speaking at the Building the Future of Health hui this week, a regular webinar to update health professionals and anyone else interested on Te Whatu's work. Hefford said the "medical cavalry" was not coming to get the country out of the shortage of general practitioners which was predicted to grow to 1000 by 2033. About 40 to 50 percent of GP work could be done by telehealth consultations, he said. "We are not going to be able to train enough doctors to cover the GP shortage that we forecast and we need to look at other ways of managing access and managing health problems and demand," he said. Telehealth is when patients have appointments with their GP via video or phone calls. Because the location of GPs did not always align with where there was the greatest need, telehealth could give more people access to care, he said. And help could come from outside of the country too. "It's a great opportunity to balance demand in rural areas, demand in areas with high need populations, with people who might be operating from anywhere in New Zealand or anywhere actually in the world, providing they are New Zealand trained or New Zealand accredited," he said. One major GP group said it was "dismayed" by the comments. Deliberate underinvestment The General Practitioners Owners Association chair Angus Chambers said it showed Te Whatu Ora did not understand the work of GPs. Telehealth was a great complement to general practice for matters that did not need face to face intervention, but there was other care that could only be achieved by being in the same room with someone, he said. That included "opportunistic care", he said. That was where doctors might notice another problem or take the chance to talk to their patients about a matter they had not come to the doctor about. He was also annoyed by Hefford's suggestion that non doctor roles play a greater part in clinical care such as nurses, health care assistants, physios and health coaches. "This is yet another example of Te Whatu Ora misunderstanding and undervaluing GPs' work. Mr Hefford also claimed that 20 percent of general practice work could be undertaken by physiotherapists. This is just ludicrous and assumes that the diagnosis has somehow been achieved without a GP," he said. Chambers told Checkpoint telehealth was "second best" for many conditions. He questioned if Te Whatu Ora was deliberately underinvesting to fix the GP shortage. "We've been warning of the workforce shortage for decades and they haven't really done anything about it. "It's well documented that they haven't covered the increase in cost of providing healthcare and we are about to lose our general practice services and the number of areas." https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/checkpoint/audio/ 2018937707/gps hit out at tele health move Telehealth was not a cheaper option in the long term, he said. People with regular access to GPs cost the system less and live longer, he said. While national coordination has improved crisis response and planning, primary care access—particularly GP appointments—has worsened for many, especially low-income and Māori/Pacific communities. The reforms replaced 20 district health boards with Health New Zealand and created a Māori Health Authority for Treaty-based governance. Central coordination strengthened winter planning and workforce equity, but failed to address affordability and accessibility issues. The 2024 decision to disband the Māori Health Authority exposed how fragile reforms are without bipartisan political backing. Structural reform alone cannot guarantee equity; success depends on funding, workforce capacity, and political stability. For most New Zealanders, the reforms' success will be judged by GP access and affordability, not organizational alignment.

[repub:theconversation] Arshad Ali and Ehtasham Ghauri Did NZ's
sweeping health reforms deliver on their promise? [the_conversation_tracker] https://counter.theconversation.com/content/ 272262/count.gif?distributor=republish-lightbox-advanced The future of NZ's health reforms now depend as much on politics as on policy. File photo. When the former Labour-led government unveiled the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) reforms in 2022, it billed them as the biggest shakeup of New Zealand's health system in a generation. The sweeping overhaul promised to end chronic fragmentation and narrow postcode-based gaps in care, and to tackle long-standing health inequities. Three years on - and with a change in government - what can we say that it delivered? We explored this question in a soon-to-be-published analysis and found that the picture is mixed. While national co-ordination has improved crisis response and planning, everyday access to primary care - especially GP appointments - has become harder for many people. The shift in political direction has also revealed a deeper lesson: structural reform can build capacity, but without durable political consensus and clear accountability, any gains in equity remain fragile. What did the reforms actually change? The reforms replaced 20 district health boards with a single national organisation, Health New Zealand, and created a Māori Health Authority to embed Treaty-based governance and commissioning. It was a major milestone in New Zealand, recognising Māori leadership in the health system and te Tiriti partnership. The aim was straightforward. A more centralised system could plan better, respond faster in crises and deliver more consistent services across the country. In some respects, we found the reforms have worked. Central co-ordination has strengthened winter planning, workforce pay equity, procurement, and the ability to move patients and resources across regions during periods of pressure. During major weather events and seasonal surges, such as Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023, the health system has been better able to function as a single, coordinated entity rather than a collection of disconnected local services. Nonetheless, these

improvements have not translated into better access to everyday
primary care, leaving a gap that is now at the centre of public concern. General practice has become the front line test of whether the reforms are working, and the 2024 decision to disband the Māori Health Authority has added a further stress test of the system's resilience. According to the 2025 Health Quality & Safety Commission survey, about one in five adults could not get care from their regular GP or nurse when they needed. This was mainly due to long waits, staff shortages or clinic closures. Delays at the primary care level push more people into emergency departments, increasing pressure on hospitals. Low-income groups, especially Māori and Pacific communities, are particularly affected, reflecting the ongoing inequities the reforms aimed to address. While some health indicators have improved after the reforms, access to primary care remains uneven, with affordability and availability continuing to determine who receives timely treatment. These figures make GP access a key indicator of whether the system is delivering on its promises. More specifically, this pattern exposes a key limitation of the reforms: centralisation can improve coordination, but it does not guarantee accessibility, affordability or a sustainable funding model for general practice. In other words, the levers that shape people's everyday experience of the system were never fully addressed. Why GP access remains the real test Those issues sit largely outside the structural changes of 2022 reforms, yet they shape how people experience the health system day to day. Equity was meant to be a central defining feature of the reforms, particularly through the establishment of the Māori Health Authority. The objective was to provide authority to Māori people in health policy-making, commissioning services, and shaping their priorities. However, the decision to disestablish the Māori Health Authority in 2024 highlighted a core challenge in New Zealand's health reforms. Supporters argue that a single system improves efficiency and clarity. Critics argue it shows equity was never securely embedded but remained politically
contingent. The Waitangi Tribunal found the Crown failed to meet its
Treaty obligations in the way the authority was revoked. Regardless of
one's political stance, the removal of this authority exposes a deeper
problem: reforms based on contested governance, without broad
political backing, are always at risk of being reversed. Consequently, the
change of government has exposed how fragile reform can be when it

lacks bipartisan backing and durable accountability mechanisms. When governance arrangements shift with each election cycle, continuity suffers, and so does public trust. None of this means the 2022 reforms were misguided. They responded to real and well-documented problems. The pre-reform system was more fragmented, inconsistent and often confusing for patients and providers alike. Centralisation has reduced duplication and improved national oversight in ways that were difficult under the old model. However, the past three years show that structural reform alone does not guarantee equity or access. Health systems transform slowly, and outcomes are shaped more by funding, workforce capacity, incentives and political stability than by organisational charts. For most New Zealanders, the success of the reforms will not be judged by how well agencies align at the centre, but by whether they can see a GP when they need one, afford that visit, and avoid ending up in hospital as a result. On that measure, the reforms remain unfinished, and their future now depends as much on politics as on policy. * Arshad Ali is a researcher at the University of Otago and Ehtasham Ghauri is a principal lecturer. 2.fileDescription: New Health NZ Te Whatu Ora Commissioner Lester Levy has been appointed to replace the board, prioritizing reducing waiting times, boosting productivity, and enhancing compassion. The organization faces a $1.3 billion deficit with $130 million monthly overspending, attributed to excessive bureaucracy, 2,500 back-office staff additions since 2018, poor procurement, and lack of oversight. Levy describes the organization as "totally bloated" with bureaucracy. The appointment sparked political debate, with the government blaming Labour's health reforms and centralization, while Labour counters that underfunding and inflation are the real issues. Health advocates warn the system is understaffed and underfunded, questioning whether budget cuts will harm frontline services.

chunkHighlights.text: 'Totally bloated': New Health NZ Te Whatu Ora boss Lester Levy lays into bureaucracy

Health NZ Te Whatu Ora's new commissioner Lester Levy. The new
Commissioner of Health NZ Te Whatu Ora says his top priority is reducing waiting times, and he also wants to boost productivity and compassion. The government on Monday announced Professor Lester Levy, who had been brought in as chair of the organisation at the end of May, would replace the board as a commissioner. Health Minister Shane Reti had said this was a response to serious concerns about oversight, overspend, and a significant deterioration in financial outlook, with Health NZ now spending $130 million a month over its budget - heading towards a $1.3b deficit by the end of the financial year. He also brought in changes to add four regional deputy chief executives, to devolve decisions on healthcare to a more local level. Levy said a lot of the government's announcement yesterday which included a lot focused on finances, but he took on the role for three reasons: wait times, productivity and compassion. "Our most urgent and critical priority is to reduce waiting times," he told reporters in Auckland on Tuesday morning. Second, a lot more healthcare could be delivered out of the resources being provided, he said. "Productivity is not an economic or financial construct .... productivity is a clinical construct." Finally, he wanted Health New Zealand to be more compassionate and caring. "We want to be consistent that every person actually gets this." He said the $1.3b deficit was "entirely unacceptable, because never before has there been so much money invested into healthcare, never before have we had so many FTEs". He said Health NZ was a big organisation, but in his view it is "totally bloated" with bureaucracy. It would be a challenge to resolve but it would be resolved, he said, and then the organisation would focus all its attention on patients. Health NZ was formed when the previous Labour government merged 20 District Health Boards, aiming to reduce costs and duplication and eliminating the 'post-code lottery' of inconsistent care across different regions. Chief executive Margie Apa said the organisation now had some resources it did not have when it
started, and to focus on delivering care in the regions. Margie Apa She

says the change will push responsibilities and accountabilities for
budgets into the regions, as well as looking at how resources and staffing was managed. Merging 29 entities was never going to be fully achieved in the first two years, Apa said - particularly when they were dealing with Covid during the first couple of years - but there was now an opportunity to ensure the different regions had a voice in the way care was delivered. Political storm rages The political rhetoric around Levy's appointment has continued to focus on who takes the blame for the budget blow-out. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon could not say exactly how much an extra 2500 back-office staff had cost, but was confident the extra bureaucracy had contributed to costs. He said the agency had a $30 billion budget to manage and that had not been done well. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon "So there's a financial performance issue, but importantly there's also an organisational performance issue in terms of what has been put together as a restructure, what has created large amounts of bureaucracy and management." Luxon said there was also a third issue - a lack of healthcare targets and outcomes. He had on Monday put the blame on the previous Labour government's approach to its health reform programme. However, Labour has continued to hit back against those accusations, saying a financial blow-out "in the financial year that they are responsible for is [the coalition's] responsibility". Labour leader Chris Hipkins told reporters at Parliament on Tuesday the government was overstating its intervention at Health New Zealand, saying the suggestion it had sacked the board was "interesting spin" given five of the seven board members had already quit. He told reporters it was a big shift in power to just one person. Labour leader Chris Hipkins "It's a bit ironic that they're saying the system has become too centralised, when they've now gone to the ultimate centralisation model where they've now got one person doing the job that used to be done by many." He said the government was manufacturing problems to justify its own Budget decisions. Health Minister Dr Shane Reti was clear in his
view Health NZ was overspending, and had a lack of oversight. He told
RNZ the overspending was due to back-office staffing, outsourcing of
personnel, poor procurement processes for supplies including inventory
on expired stock, as well as inflation and population growth. It included
things like 2500 administrative backoffice staff being added to the
payroll since 2018 with no notable improvements to the health metrics,

he said - and part of the problem had been that no one was watching.
"This is what the Office of the Auditor General said as well .... there was no internal performance monitoring framework, no one was looking, no one was watching until it became so bad that it suddenly raised a flag up the flag pole and Health NZ became aware of this." Health Minister Shane Reti He said some of the recruitment had been into areas where it was needed least, and not into priority areas such as mental health, maternity, and critical care. Health New Zealand also had not been sharing financial information and board papers with the ministry, he said. "Part of the issue was Health NZ wasn't sharing. They refused to share information with the Minister, and with the Ministry of Health, and actually with Treasury. "Minister Willis and I had to be quite firm early in this year: 'you will share information with your legislative steward the ministry of health, oh, and by the way, with Treasury." In a statement issued as National's spokesperson for Health, Dr Reti claimed Labour was "reinventing history". "This is not a matter of there not being enough funding," he said. "When National and Labour released their strategy for health in the 2023 election, both parties had exactly the same figure - an additional $12.57 billion for Health NZ over the forecast period. National has gone even further and invested a record $16.7 billion in the [three budgets to 2026] for Health New Zealand, plus an additional $604 million for more medicines." However, Labour's Ayesha Verrall said this was a major misunderstanding of his own Budget. "Following the election, new estimates of cost inflation and of population growth were made and those were not funded by this government - that's why there's a deficit." She said the government owed the public an explanation, and perhaps Health NZ should reinstate the DHB approach of publishing monthly accounts and the breakdown of staff and costs. The board meetings should also be public, she said. Labour's health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall "I have said repeatedly that those meetings should be public, they were made public while Labour was in government and then they reverted to being predominantly in private
since the government's changed, which is odd because Shane Reti
campaigned on them being public as well." Asked about Levy's track
record, she said she would judge him on the job he had been appointed
to now. "I'm not in the habit of slagging off public servants who decide to
do service for our country. I think the exiting board of Te Whatu Ora has
been treated shabbily, I am going to judge Lester Levy on the decisions

he makes in this role now." Health advocates warn of underfunding
Executive director Sarah Dalton, from the Association of Senior Medical Specialists senior doctors union, questioned the government's $130m a month overspend claim, saying her organisation saw an understaffed system. Association of Senior Medical Specialists executive director Sarah Dalton "I'm in the middle of meetings with our members all over the country, and there is not a single service that is well staffed and that is able to provide the kind of care the people of New Zealand want and expect to be able to access in our health system. So taking to our health budgets with an axe does not seem an appropriate response when we do not have enough doctors, nurses, or allied health workers or the people who support them to do their work." She said the health system was not adequately funded, which was a major part of the problem. Her organisation had done a "deep dive" into this year's health budget provisions and found there was very little new money, with lots of smoke and mirrors in the way it had been presented. Former chair of Te Whatu Ora Rob Campbell - who was fired from the agency's board last year after making politicised comments about the National Party - said he agreed with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon that they could not keep putting money into a system which was not working. He said the issues in Te Whatu Ora were, however, much wider than just financial or governance control. Campbell said he believed there were issues of mis-management and underfunding, but the government should be looking at the Ministry of Health to find out why the system was not working. He said the Ministry of Health was the key element in setting targets for Te Whatu Ora, setting its budget and allocating money, and had presided over the running-down of the health system over many years. It had now devised and was running the new system, he said. "The Minister of Health remains the steward of the new system and the key element in setting policy and the amount of funding that is available. The Ministry of Health is the place they should be looking to say 'why isn't this working, and why haven't we been told'." Rob
Campbell Verrall said the issue came back to the government's choices,
and this year's Budget did not fund the health system in line with
inflation. "Predictably, in a country with increasing population and
inflation in the health sector, they are now behind where they need to be
in terms of funding the health system to keep up with demand." She said
it was impossible to cut $1.4b without affecting frontline services.

3.fileDescription: A Deloitte consultant report reveals that Health New Zealand lost control of spending, contributing to a dramatic financial collapse from a projected $500 million surplus to over $1 billion deficit in 2023/24. The report identifies critical failures including missing financial plans, lack of executive and board-level controls, ineffective savings programs, inaccurate budgeting, and poor communication between central and regional teams. Key issues include operational teams ignoring cost-saving directives, staff turnover undermining financial controls, and regional teams approving extra hires based on mistaken beliefs about available funding. The report suggests the previous 20 district health boards had better financial planning. Health Minister Simeon Brown announced major reforms including a new board structure, localized health services, and $285 million additional funding for GPs over three years to address systemic mismanagement.

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's society across multiple dimensions. It covers the nation's diverse population of over 5 million people, including 67% of European descent, significant Māori (565,329), Pacific Islander, and Asian communities. Demographic trends reveal an aging population, declining birth rates, and increasing ethnic diversity concentrated primarily in the North Island, particularly Auckland. The document details family structures, housing trends showing declining home ownership (from 73.8% in 1991 to 67.8% in 2001), and rising single-parent families (31% in 2001). Gender dynamics highlight women's improved economic and social status since the 1980s, alongside New Zealand's progressive LGBTQ+ rights stance, including decriminalization of homosexuality (1986), civil unions (2005), and same-sex marriage (2013). Health outcomes have improved significantly since the 1950s, with life expectancy at 76 years for men and 81 for women (2000), though Māori populations experience lower life expectancy and higher mortality rates. The education system provides free, compulsory state schooling from ages 6-16, with special initiatives like kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa Māori for language preservation. Religion remains important with approximately half the population identifying as Christian, though church attendance is low and religious diversity has increased through immigration. The document traces cultural evolution including the transformation of cuisine from British traditions to cosmopolitan cooking, beverage consumption shifts from beer to wine and coffee, and relaxed dress codes reflecting global influences. Throughout, it highlights both multicultural achievements and persistent socioeconomic disparities faced by Māori communities.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of primary health care and the medical profession in New Zealand from 1867 to the early 21st century. It documents the transformation from family doctors, nurses, and midwives delivering care in the 1800s, through professionalization and self-regulation (Medical Practitioners' Act 1867, nursing registration 1901, midwifery registration 1911), to the modern primary health care system. Key developments include district nursing services, Plunket (1907), and the 1941 agreement maintaining fee-for-service payments with government subsidies. The document examines challenges of a two-tiered system with free hospital care but expensive GP visits, and traces reform efforts from the 1970s onwards, including midwife autonomy re-establishment (1990), alternative practitioners' emergence, and patient rights activism. Major reforms in the 1990s-2000s introduced contractual arrangements with GPs, independent practitioner associations (IPAs), and primary health organisations (PHOs) based on population-based funding with higher subsidies for disadvantaged populations. The 2015 zero-fee GP visits scheme for children under 13 represents the latest access initiative. The document also details Māori health care practices combining natural medicines and spiritual healing with European medicine.

chunkHighlights.text: Improving access

In the early 20th century many people joined friendly societies, which provided medical care to their members. The first Labour government (from 1935) wanted to give all New Zealanders free health care. They planned to pay GPs a fixed rate for all consultations, but GPs opposed this. Instead they were paid by the government for each consultation, and could charge an extra fee as well. Over time GPs increased their fees to patients.

6.fileDescription: Te Whatu Ora director Martin Hefford claims 40-50% of GP work could be delivered via telehealth, including by overseas-trained doctors, to address New Zealand's predicted GP shortage of 1000 by 2033. However, the General Practitioners Owners Association chair Angus Chambers expressed dismay, arguing telehealth cannot replace face-to-face care for opportunistic care and complex diagnoses. Chambers criticized the suggestion that non-doctor roles could undertake significant clinical work, calling it "ludicrous." He questioned whether Te Whatu Ora was deliberately underinvesting in GP services. ByRowan Quinn - Senior Journalist
2024-05-09 16:24:06+12:00

Te Whatu Ora director of living well Martin Hefford says 40 to 50 percent
of GP work could be done by telehealth consultations. A Te Whatu Ora/ Health NZ boss says up to half of all GP work could be done by telehealth - including by overseas-based doctors. Martin Hefford The agency's director of living well Martin Hefford was speaking at the Building the Future of Health hui this week, a regular webinar to update health professionals - and anyone else interested - on Te Whatu's work. Hefford said the "medical cavalry" was not coming to get the country out of the shortage of general practitioners which was predicted to grow to 1000 by 2033. About 40 to 50 percent of GP work could be done by telehealth consultations, he said. "We are not going to be able to train enough doctors to cover the GP shortage that we forecast and we need to look at other ways of managing access and managing health problems and demand," he said. Telehealth is when patients have appointments with their GP via video or phone calls. Because the location of GPs did not always align with where there was the greatest need, telehealth could give more people access to care, he said. And help could come from outside of the country too. "It's a great opportunity to balance demand in rural areas, demand in areas with high need populations, with people who might be operating from anywhere in New Zealand or anywhere actually in the world, providing they are New Zealand trained or New Zealand accredited," he said. One major GP group said it was "dismayed" by the comments. Deliberate underinvestment The General Practitioners Owners Association chair Angus Chambers said it showed Te Whatu Ora did not understand the work of GPs. Telehealth was a great complement to general practice for matters that did not need face to face intervention, but there was other care that could only be achieved by being in the same room with someone, he said. That included "opportunistic care", he said. That was where doctors might notice another problem or take the chance to talk to their patients about a matter they had not come to the doctor about.
He was also annoyed by Hefford's suggestion that non-doctor roles play

a greater part in clinical care - such as nurses, health care assistants,
physios and health coaches. "This is yet another example of Te Whatu Ora misunderstanding and undervaluing GPs' work. Mr Hefford also claimed that 20 percent of general practice work could be undertaken by physiotherapists. This is just ludicrous and assumes that the diagnosis has somehow been achieved without a GP," he said. Chambers told Checkpoint telehealth was "second best" for many conditions. He questioned if Te Whatu Ora was deliberately underinvesting to fix the GP shortage. "We've been warning of the workforce shortage for decades and they haven't really done anything about it. "It's well documented that they haven't covered the increase in cost of providing healthcare and we are about to lose our general practice services and the number of areas." https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/checkpoint/audio/ 2018937707/gps-hit-out-at-tele-health-move Telehealth was not a cheaper option in the long term, he said. People with regular access to GPs cost the system less and live longer, he said. "One might wonder if the system doesn't want people to live longer because they cost a lot more once they get over 65 but that might be a cynical view." However, he said telehealth was useful for people in remote areas. It worked during the Covid-19 pandemic, but people flocked back to clinics once they could "because they actually like human contact", Chambers said. Hefford said there were 21 million "GP engagements" in New Zealand last year. About 5 million New Zealanders, or 96 percent of the population were enrolled with a clinic. But for the rest there were still barriers to care, such as being able to get an appointment or not being able to afford to go. Work had to be done to break those barriers down, and find new ways to make sure everyone got the care they needed as doctor numbers shrank. However, Health New Zealand said greater use of telehealth services would "free up" GPs to focus on complex patients. The National Clinical Director of Primary Care, Dr Sarah Clarke, said the agency was working hard to boost the GP workforce with extra funding and training places - but there critical shortages remained. "Despite our
best efforts, we still don't have enough GPs, and we will have to work
together as a system to redirect some of the tasks GPs do so they can
focus their time on the complex care that is done best by our valued GP
workforce," she said in a written response to RNZ. "We know that
continuity of care in general practice is important, and that being with
the same provider for at least 15 years significantly reduces the risk of

death, the need for acute care after hours, and hospital admissions. In a model where you know your patient, continuity can be maintained while a lot of care is provided via telehealth, as is already happening right across Aotearoa." Many practices were already providing a large number of services via telehealth, such as letting patients check test results or request prescriptions online, she said. "We use telehealth every day, as it is one way to provide quality care that is efficient and convenient for people, their whānau and for communities." Te Whatu Ora defined "telehealth" in this broader sense, not simply video or telephone consultations, she said. Related

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines health inequalities and social determinants of health in New Zealand, focusing on disparities among ethnic groups. It explores how socio-economic status, ethnicity, employment, housing, education, and environmental conditions shape health outcomes. Significant health disparities exist between Māori and Pākehā populations, with Māori experiencing lower life expectancy (73-77 years vs 80-84 years in 2012-14), and an 8-year gap between least and most deprived areas for males. Major health challenges include cancer (30% of deaths in 2015), cardiovascular diseases, tobacco use, poor nutrition, and obesity. Tobacco remains the leading preventable cause of death, with Māori adults 2.5 times more likely to smoke. Healthcare access is limited by cost, with 25-33% deferring doctor visits due to expense. The document traces New Zealand's health services evolution from fee-based systems (pre-1940s) to subsidized services (post-1938) and the 21st-century primary health organization model. It discusses culturally responsive healthcare approaches for Māori and Pacific populations, including decorated clinics and traditional healer referrals. While Asian populations showed better health outcomes, they faced language barriers. Government policy and district health boards made reducing inequalities a statutory obligation, though targeted public health initiatives have not reached all eligible populations.

chunkHighlights.text: Because New Zealand’s primary health service was partly funded by patient fees, cost still limited access to GPs in the 21st century. Women were more likely to defer visits than men because they had less disposable income.

10.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of insurance in New Zealand from early colonial times through the early 21st century, covering life insurance, general insurance, accident insurance, and disaster coverage. Early colonial New Zealand faced significant risks including shipwrecks, fires, and workplace accidents, driving rapid insurance industry growth. The government established Government Life Insurance in 1869 and State Fire Insurance Office in 1903 to provide affordable coverage. The document details accident insurance development from the early 1900s, motor vehicle insurance following widespread car availability, and the 1972 Accident Compensation Commission that replaced litigation. Disaster insurance evolution is examined through major events including the 1931 Napier earthquake and creation of the Earthquake and War Damage Commission (1944), later becoming the Natural Hazards Commission in 2024. The 20th century witnessed significant structural transformations including the shift from commission agents to insurance brokers, blurring of boundaries between life and general insurance sectors, and major takeovers and privatization following 1980s economic reforms. Government Life became Tower Corporation and was eventually privatized, while State Insurance was sold to Norwich Union Holdings. Modern developments saw branch offices decline as telephone and internet services replaced face-to-face interactions. By 2007-8, the industry earned over $3 billion in gross income, with general insurance premiums exceeding $3 billion and life insurance premiums reaching $1.48 billion.

13.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the history of dental care in New Zealand from early Polynesian times through the 21st century. It covers the evolution of Māori oral health, which improved after 1500 CE due to dietary changes, contrasted with poor Pākehā dental health in the 19th century. Key developments include the introduction of foot-pedal dental engines from the 1870s, nitrous oxide for pain relief, and professional dentist registration from 1880. The Otago University dental school was established in 1907. The document details the division between "mechanical dentists" and "ethical dentists," the formation of the New Zealand Dental Association in 1905, and the establishment of the School Dental Service (SDS) in 1921—a world-first state-funded initiative. It chronicles the SDS's expansion, the transition from dental nurses to dental therapists in the 1990s, and the evolution into the Community Oral Health Service. The document highlights Professor John Walsh's transformative leadership at Otago's dental school (1946-1971), technological advances including high-speed drills and X-rays, and the introduction of dental hygienists and therapists. Modern dentistry emphasizes prevention and tooth preservation. The document addresses persistent challenges including oral health disparities among Māori and Pasifika communities, the water fluoridation debate introduced in Hastings in 1953, and cost barriers to adult dental care.
